cards.text: The poet is still grieving over Zion, another name for Jerusalem. He opens this poem with one heavy word: "How." And the first thing he points to is the gold.

cards.question: The poet looks at Zion's pure gold. What has happened to it?

cards.text: And the gems of the temple lie scattered on every street corner. Friend, I lost my shine in the back of a junk drawer and thought THAT was rough, but this is a whole city.

cards.question: The precious sons of Zion were once worth their weight in pure ___. Now they are esteemed as jars of ___, the work of a potter's hands.
Zion's sons went from pure gold to ordinary clay jars. What is the poet saying about how they're seen now?

answers.text: They are seen as cheap and common
They are seen as strong and useful
They are seen as dangerous and wild

cards.text: Then the poet looks out to the wilderness, where even jackals nurse their young.

cards.question: Even jackals nurse their young. But the poet says the daughter of his people has become ___, like an ostrich in the wilderness.

cards.text: The nursing infant is so thirsty his tongue clings to the roof of his mouth.

cards.question: When the little children in Zion beg for bread, someone gives them some.
The poet says those who once ate delicacies are destitute in the streets, and those brought up in crimson huddle in ash heaps. What is he showing?

answers.text: The poor have finally been fed
The people have moved to the country

cards.text: Then the poet brings up Sodom, the city the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on (Genesis 19:24). Sodom was overthrown in an instant, without a hand turned to help her.

cards.question: The poet says the punishment of the daughter of his people is greater than Sodom's.

cards.text: Now the poet remembers the city's dignitaries. They were brighter than snow, whiter than milk, more ruddy than rubies.

cards.question: Zion's dignitaries were once brighter than snow. What does the poet say their appearance is like now?
People still recognize Zion's dignitaries when they see them in the streets.

cards.text: Their skin has shriveled on their bones. It's as dry as a stick.

cards.question: The poet says some people waste away, pierced with pain, because the fields lack produce. Who does he say are better off than those who die of hunger?

answers.text: Those who hid in the hills

cards.text: Then comes the hardest line in this poem, friend, so I'll just say it plainly. The poet says, "The hands of compassionate women have cooked their own children," in the destruction of his people.

cards.question: The poet says the ___ kindled a fire in Zion that consumed her foundations.

cards.text: Now the poet steps back and looks at the whole world. The kings of the earth did not believe, and neither did any people of the world, that an enemy could ever enter the gates of Jerusalem.

cards.question: But the enemy got in. The poet says it was for the sins of those who shed the blood of the righteous in Jerusalem. Who were they?

cards.text: Those prophets and priests wandered blind in the streets, defiled by that blood. No one dared to touch their garments.

cards.question: When the defiled prophets and priests come near, men shout at them, "Go away! ___!"
When the prophets and priests flee and wander among the nations, they're welcomed to stay.

cards.text: The poet says the presence of the LORD has scattered them. He regards them no more.

cards.question: How are Zion's priests and elders treated now?

answers.text: With no honor and no favor
With honor for their long service

cards.text: Then the poet says, "All the while our eyes were failing as we looked in vain for help." I know that look, friend: every time my drawer opened I thought THIS was my ride, and it was just somebody grabbing the tape.

cards.question: The nation the people watched for from their towers was able to save them.

cards.text: Meanwhile the enemy stalked their every step, so they couldn't even walk in their own streets. The poet says their end had come.

cards.question: The poet says the ones who chased his people were swifter than what?

cards.text: They pursued them over the mountains and ambushed them in the wilderness. Faster than EAGLES, friend, and I'm a stamper hopping around on a gold base, so I'd have been caught before I made it past the oven.
Then the poet names another painful loss: "The LORD’s anointed, the breath of our life, was captured in their pits."

cards.question: The people had high hopes for the LORD's anointed before he was captured. What had they said about him?

answers.text: They would live under his shadow
He would rebuild the temple walls
He would make them rich again

cards.text: Then the poet turns to Edom, the nation that came from Esau (Genesis 36:9). He says, "So rejoice and be glad, O Daughter of Edom, you who dwell in the land of Uz."

cards.question: Yet the poet says the ___ will pass to Edom as well, and she will get drunk and expose herself.

cards.text: Then the poet turns back and speaks to the Daughter of Zion one last time.

cards.question: The poet tells the Daughter of Zion that her punishment is complete.
The poet says the LORD will punish the iniquity of the Daughter of Edom. What will He do with her sins?

cards.text: And for Zion, the poet says He will not prolong her exile. After a whole poem of dark, friend, that's a slice of light coming through the drawer.

findings.problem: Verse 11 opens with "The LORD has exhausted His wrath; He has poured out His fierce anger," and no card tells it. The only verse 11 card asks who kindled the fire. The LORD's wrath is a key detail for understanding the whole poem, and the baker never hears it.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: No story card sets up this question. The card before it is about verse 10, the women and their children. Without the wrath lines from verse 11, "enemy" is just as reasonable a pick as "LORD" for who set a fire in a conquered city, so the baker can only guess.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: Card 8 quotes "we looked in vain for help," and the joke ends with the drawer opening for nothing ("it was just somebody grabbing the tape"). Together they give away the answer to the true or false on card 9, which asks whether the nation they watched for was able to save them.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: "Swifter than what?" asks the baker to guess a detail of the poet's image (eagles, horses or lions). Nothing earlier lets the baker reason it out. This matches the Psalm 23 bad example, which asks what David's head is anointed with.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: "The LORD's anointed" first appears here, and the card never says who that is. The baker isn't told it means the king, so the loss, and the question on card 14, are hard to follow.

rule.text: The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The card says the poet "turns back and speaks to the Daughter of Zion one last time." That suggests he has spoken to her directly earlier in this poem. Verse 22 is the only place in Lamentations 4 where he addresses the Daughter of Zion directly. Earlier verses speak about "the daughter of my people" instead.

rule.text: What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: "He will not prolong your exile" comes before the lines about Edom in verse 22. This card tells it after the Edom question on card 19. That moves backward in the passage and changes how it ends: the text ends on Edom's sins being exposed, not on hope for Zion.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.
